# What I would change

## The backend, honestly

- Turing.jl gave us submodels, a choice of samplers, and the rest of
  Julia. The proof of concept exists because of it, and choosing it was
  right at the time
- It is still 0.x. First release in 2017, current release v0.46.0 in
  July 2026
- Ten breaking releases between v0.37.0 and v0.46.0 in eighteen months.
  The submodel interface change left our own language incompatible with
  the current release
- Since February, one person has written 17 of the commits to Turing.jl
  and 47 of the commits to DynamicPPL.jl, where most of the composition
  machinery lives. Nobody else is above nine

::: {.callout-important}
This is not a criticism of the people doing the work, which is good
work. It is a statement about how much of the stack rests on very few
of them.
:::

::: {.attribution}
Counts from the GitHub API on 2026-08-10, `main` branches, human
authors only.
:::

## Automatic differentiation is the part that decided it

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
- Turing is tested most extensively against four backends. Everything
  else routes through `DifferentiationInterface.jl`
- `ADTests`, the one public table of which backends worked with which
  Turing models, was archived in June 2026 and has not been replaced
- So we run our own matrix in CI. Six backends per package, each with
  its own badge and its own coverage flag
- We also keep a package whose entire job is holding gradient
  workarounds until the upstream fix lands, and then deleting them
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.callout-important}
## From the Turing.jl documentation
"not all AD libraries in there are thoroughly tested on Turing models.
Thus, it is possible that some of them will either error ... or maybe
even silently give incorrect results"
:::

- For a model somebody acts on during an outbreak, a silently wrong
  gradient is not a footnote
